paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of quantity
paragraphs.text: A quantity that is measured by a number can be one of two kinds: continuous or discrete. A continuous variable can take two values and every value lying between them, so there is always another possibility in between. A discrete variable works differently. Around each value it can take, there is a gap of real size on both sides holding no allowed values. Some variables are even discrete over one stretch of the number line and continuous over another.

paragraphs.heading: Counting the allowed values
paragraphs.text: Another way to say it: a variable is discrete exactly when its values can be paired off, one to one, with some of the natural numbers. For any allowed value, there is a smallest positive distance to the next allowed one. The count of allowed values is either finite or countably infinite. Typical cases are variables that must be whole numbers, non-negative whole numbers, positive whole numbers, or just 0 and 1.

paragraphs.heading: Why the difference matters
paragraphs.text: In statistics the two kinds count as separate data types, and each is described by its own sort of probability distribution. For a discrete variable, the distribution can be written as a probability mass function; for a continuous one, as a probability density function. Calculus is often used when variables are continuous, but it does not fit problems with discrete variables so easily. Integer programming is one kind of problem built on discrete variables.

paragraphs.heading: Time in steps
paragraphs.text: Time itself can be treated either way. When time flows continuously, the equation for how something changes over time is a differential equation. When time moves in separate steps, that equation is called a difference equation instead. For some discrete-time systems, the difference equation can be solved for an analytical solution that models how the system responds.

paragraphs.heading: The 0-1 switch
paragraphs.text: A variable allowed only the values 0 and 1 is called a dummy variable. It acts like a switch, turning parts of an equation on or off by giving the two values to different parameters. In regression analysis it can mark subgroups of a sample, with 0 standing, for instance, for someone in the control group. When the outcome being predicted is itself a dummy variable, logistic or probit regression is the usual choice.

paragraphs.heading: When both kinds mix
paragraphs.text: Some models hold both kinds at once, such as a variable x that is only 0 or 1 next to a continuous variable y. A single random variable can be mixed too, and waiting in a queue is an example. The chance of waiting no time at all is a discrete piece, while any wait longer than zero is measured on a continuous time scale. The cumulative distribution function of such a mixed variable is neither purely discrete nor continuous everywhere.
